subject: Physics
title: Polar Satellites
description: Satellites in a low-altitude orbit that passes over or near the Earth's North and South poles, allowing them to scan the entire planet's surface over successive orbits.
learning_objectives: Describe a polar orbit
Explain how a polar satellite can observe the entire surface of the Earth over time
Compare polar orbits with geostationary orbits in terms of altitude, period, and typical use
explanation: A polar satellite orbits the Earth in a path that passes over, or very close to, the North and South poles, rather than around the equator as a geostationary satellite does. Polar orbits are typically at a much lower altitude than geostationary orbits, and therefore have a much shorter orbital period (often around 90 to 100 minutes). Because the Earth itself rotates on its axis beneath the satellite's orbit, and the orbital plane of a polar satellite stays roughly fixed in space while the Earth rotates underneath it, each successive orbit passes over a different strip of the Earth's surface; over the course of many orbits (typically completing a full coverage cycle within about a day), a polar satellite can scan and image the entire surface of the planet, including the polar regions that a geostationary satellite (fixed above the equator) cannot usefully observe. This makes polar orbits especially well suited to global mapping, environmental and climate monitoring, and reconnaissance applications requiring complete surface coverage.
key_concepts: Orbits pass near/over the North and South poles
Lower altitude, shorter period than geostationary satellites
Earth's rotation beneath the fixed orbital plane gives full surface coverage over time

definitions.definition: A satellite orbit that passes over or near the Earth's North and South poles, allowing coverage of the entire planet's surface as the Earth rotates beneath the orbit.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why a polar satellite is able to observe the entire surface of the Earth over a series of orbits, even though each individual orbit only passes over a narrow strip of the planet.
steps: The satellite's orbital plane remains roughly fixed relative to distant space as it orbits.
Meanwhile, the Earth continues to rotate on its axis beneath the satellite's orbit.
Because of this rotation, each successive orbit of the satellite passes over a different north-south strip of the Earth's surface, slightly shifted from the previous orbit.
Over many orbits (as the Earth completes a full rotation), the satellite's accumulated ground track covers the entire surface of the planet.
worked_examples.answer: Because the Earth rotates beneath the satellite's roughly fixed orbital plane, each orbit covers a different strip of the surface, and over time these strips combine to cover the whole planet.

practical_applications: Global weather and climate monitoring satellites
Earth mapping and environmental monitoring, including deforestation and ice sheet tracking
Military and civilian reconnaissance satellites requiring global coverage
common_mistakes: Assuming a polar orbit and a geostationary orbit serve the same purpose, or have similar altitudes and periods
Forgetting that a single orbit of a polar satellite only covers a narrow strip, not the whole planet at once
misconceptions: That a polar satellite images the entire Earth's surface within a single orbit — each individual orbit only passes over one narrow, roughly north-south strip of the Earth; complete global coverage is only achieved cumulatively, after many orbits, as the Earth's rotation shifts each successive strip to a new location.
tips: Contrast polar orbits (low altitude, short period, full global coverage over time, fixed orbital plane relative to space) directly with geostationary orbits (high altitude, ~24-hour period, fixed position relative to the ground) to keep the two concepts clearly distinct.

basic: State the region of the Earth that a polar orbit passes over or near.
intermediate: Explain why polar satellites are well suited to global environmental monitoring.
advanced: Explain why a polar satellite typically has a much shorter orbital period than a geostationary satellite.

exam_questions: Explain how a polar-orbiting satellite is able to provide complete coverage of the Earth's surface over time, despite each individual orbital pass covering only a narrow strip.

basic: The North and South poles.
intermediate: Because a polar satellite passes over the entire range of latitudes on each orbit, and the Earth rotates beneath it, the satellite's accumulated coverage over many orbits includes the whole planet, making it well suited to tracking global environmental changes such as ice sheet extent, deforestation, or weather patterns everywhere on Earth, not just one fixed region.
advanced: Polar satellites typically orbit at a much lower altitude than geostationary satellites; since orbital speed and period both depend on orbital radius (via v = root(GM/r) and the relationship between speed, radius, and period), a smaller orbital radius results in a shorter orbital period, giving polar satellites periods of around 90-100 minutes compared with the roughly 24-hour period of a geostationary satellite.
exam: As the polar satellite completes each individual orbit, it passes over a narrow, roughly north-south strip of the Earth's surface; because the satellite's orbital plane stays roughly fixed in space while the Earth continues rotating beneath it, each successive orbit's strip is shifted slightly relative to the previous one, and after enough orbits (as the Earth completes a full rotation), these shifted strips combine to give complete coverage of the entire surface of the planet.

summary: A polar satellite orbits over or near the Earth's poles at low altitude with a short period. As the Earth rotates beneath its roughly fixed orbital plane, successive orbits cover different strips of the surface, together providing complete global coverage over time.
revision_notes: Passes over/near the poles; low altitude, short period (~90-100 min)
Earth rotates beneath fixed orbital plane -> full global coverage over time
Used for mapping, environmental monitoring, reconnaissance

subject: Physics
title: Gravitational Force
description: The attractive force that exists between any two objects that have mass.
learning_objectives: Describe gravitational force as a universal, always-attractive force between masses
Explain how gravitational force depends on mass and distance
Identify examples of gravitational force at different scales
explanation: Gravitational force is the attractive force that exists between any two objects that have mass, pulling them toward each other. Unlike some other forces, gravitational force is always attractive (never repulsive) and acts between every pair of masses in the universe, however small, though its effect is only noticeable for objects with very large mass, such as planets, stars, and moons, since gravitational force between everyday objects (such as two people standing near each other) is far too small to detect without extremely sensitive equipment. Gravitational force is responsible for keeping planets in orbit around the Sun, moons in orbit around planets, and objects held to the surface of the Earth (experienced as weight). The exact size of the gravitational force between two objects depends on both of their masses and the distance between them, as described quantitatively by Newton's law of gravitation, covered in its own topic.
key_concepts: Always attractive, acts between any two masses
Noticeable only for very large masses (planets, stars)
Depends on mass and distance (Newton's law of gravitation)

definitions.definition: The universal, always-attractive force that exists between any two objects that have mass.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why two people standing near each other do not notice any gravitational attraction between them, even though gravitational force technically exists between any two masses.
steps: Gravitational force exists between any two masses, including two people.
However, gravitational force is extremely small unless at least one of the objects involved has a very large mass (such as a planet).

Since human bodies have a relatively very small mass compared with astronomical objects, the gravitational force between two people is far too small to be felt or detected without highly sensitive scientific instruments.
worked_examples.answer: The gravitational force between two people does exist, but is far too small to detect directly, since neither person has anywhere near the mass required (such as that of a planet) to produce a noticeable gravitational effect.

practical_applications: Explaining planetary and lunar orbits throughout the solar system
Understanding weight and why objects fall toward the Earth
Precision experiments (such as torsion balance experiments) used to measure gravitational force directly in a laboratory
common_mistakes: Assuming gravitational force only exists for very large objects, rather than existing (but being negligibly small) between all masses
Confusing gravitational force with weight, which is specifically the gravitational force acting on an object due to a nearby large body such as the Earth
misconceptions: That gravitational force can be repulsive under certain conditions — as far as classical (non-relativistic) physics is concerned, gravitational force between masses is always attractive, pulling objects toward each other, never pushing them apart.
tips: Remember that gravitational force technically exists between every pair of masses in the universe, but is only significant (and therefore noticeable or important) when at least one of the masses involved is extremely large, such as a planet or star.

basic: State whether gravitational force is attractive, repulsive, or can be either.
intermediate: Explain why the gravitational force between the Earth and the Sun is far more significant than the gravitational force between two nearby buildings.
advanced: Explain why astronauts in orbit still experience a significant gravitational force from the Earth, even though they appear to be 'weightless'.

exam_questions: Describe gravitational force, and explain why its effects are only noticeable for objects with very large mass.

basic: Always attractive.
intermediate: The Sun (and to a lesser extent the Earth) has an enormously greater mass than either of the two buildings, and since gravitational force depends strongly on the masses involved, the resulting gravitational force between the Earth and the Sun is vastly larger and more significant than the negligible gravitational force between two ordinary buildings.
advanced: Astronauts in low Earth orbit are still well within the Earth's significant gravitational field, and this gravitational force is what provides the centripetal force keeping them in orbit; the sensation of 'weightlessness' arises because both the astronaut and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together around the Earth, not because gravity has become negligible or absent.
exam: Gravitational force is the universal, always-attractive force that exists between any two objects with mass; its effects are only noticeable for objects with very large mass because the size of the gravitational force is proportional to the product of the two masses involved, and for everyday objects (with relatively tiny mass compared with planets and stars), this product — and therefore the resulting force — is far too small to detect without extremely sensitive instruments.

summary: Gravitational force is the universal, always-attractive force between any two masses. It is significant only for very large masses, such as planets and stars, and is responsible for weight, orbits, and the large-scale structure of the universe.
revision_notes: Always attractive, exists between all masses
Only noticeable for very large masses
Responsible for weight, orbits, planetary motion

subject: Physics
title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
description: The equation describing the gravitational force between two point masses, proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
learning_objectives: State Newton's law of gravitation and its equation
Calculate the gravitational force between two masses given their separation
Explain how gravitational force changes as the distance between two masses changes
explanation: Newton's law of gravitation states that the gravitational force of attraction between any two point masses is directly proportional to the product of their masses, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. This is expressed by the equation F = Gm1m2/r^2, where m1 and m2 are the two masses, r is the distance between their centres, and G is the gravitational constant, a fixed value (approximately 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2) that determines the overall strength of gravity throughout the universe. The 'inverse square' relationship means gravitational force falls off very rapidly with increasing distance: doubling the distance between two masses reduces the gravitational force between them to one quarter of its original value, while tripling the distance reduces it to one ninth. This equation applies exactly for point masses (or, equivalently, for any spherically symmetric object, treating its entire mass as if concentrated at its centre, measuring distance from that centre), and provides the theoretical foundation for orbital motion, weight, and gravitational field strength.
key_concepts: F = Gm1m2/r^2
Inverse square law: doubling distance quarters the force
G is a universal constant, same everywhere

definitions.definition: The gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, F = Gm1m2/r^2.
A universal physical constant, approximately 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2, determining the overall strength of gravitational force between masses.

variables.r: distance between the centres of the two masses, m

worked_examples.problem: Calculate the gravitational force between two masses of 500 kg and 800 kg, with their centres separated by 2 m (use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2).
steps: Use F = Gm1m2/r^2.

practical_applications: Calculating gravitational forces between astronomical bodies (planets, moons, stars)
Determining satellite orbital parameters and mission trajectories
Precision measurements of G in laboratory experiments, such as the Cavendish experiment
common_mistakes: Forgetting to square the distance, r, in the denominator
Confusing the gravitational constant, G, with gravitational field strength, g, which are related but distinct quantities with very different values and units
misconceptions: That gravitational force decreases in direct (linear) proportion to distance — Newton's law of gravitation is an inverse SQUARE law, meaning force decreases much more rapidly than distance increases; doubling the distance reduces the force to a quarter, not to a half.
tips: Always square the distance before dividing, and double-check whether a problem is asking for a change resulting from a change in distance (using the inverse square relationship as a ratio) or a full numerical calculation using the equation directly.

basic: State Newton's law of gravitation as an equation, defining each symbol.
intermediate: Two masses experience a gravitational force of 4 x 10^-5 N at a certain separation. Calculate the new force if the separation is doubled, with the masses unchanged.
advanced: Calculate the gravitational force between the Earth (mass 6.0 x 10^24 kg) and a 70 kg person standing on its surface, at a distance of 6.4 x 10^6 m from the Earth's centre (use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2), and compare this with the person's weight calculated using W = mg.

exam_questions: Explain, using Newton's law of gravitation, why the gravitational force between two objects decreases rapidly as the distance between them increases.

basic: F = Gm1m2/r^2, where F is gravitational force in N, G is the gravitational constant, m1 and m2 are the two masses in kg, and r is the distance between their centres in m.
intermediate: Since force is inversely proportional to the square of distance, doubling the distance reduces the force to 1/(2^2) = 1/4 of its original value: new force = 4x10^-5 / 4 = 1x10^-5 N.
advanced: F = (6.67x10^-11)(6.0x10^24)(70) / (6.4x10^6)^2 = 2.8014x10^13 / 4.096x10^13 approx 684 N. Using W = mg = 70 x 9.8 = 686 N, these two values are very close (the small difference is due to rounding), confirming that gravitational force calculated from Newton's law of gravitation matches the everyday weight equation.
exam: Because gravitational force is inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the distance (F is proportional to 1/r^2), any increase in distance causes a much larger decrease in force than a simple, direct (linear) relationship would produce — for example, doubling the distance reduces the force to only a quarter of its original value, not to half, because the distance term is squared in the denominator of the equation.

summary: Newton's law of gravitation states that gravitational force between two masses is F = Gm1m2/r^2, directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. This inverse square relationship means force falls off rapidly with increasing distance.
revision_notes: F = Gm1m2/r^2
G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2 (universal constant)
Inverse square law: double distance -> force / 4

subject: Physics
title: Gravitational Field Strength
description: The gravitational force acting per unit mass at a point in a gravitational field, describing the strength of gravity at that location.
learning_objectives: Define gravitational field strength and state its unit
Calculate gravitational field strength at a point around a spherical mass using Newton's law of gravitation
Explain how gravitational field strength varies with distance from a mass
explanation: Gravitational field strength, given the symbol g, is defined as the gravitational force acting per unit mass at a particular point within a gravitational field, calculated as g = F/m, where F is the gravitational force experienced by a small test mass, m, placed at that point. Gravitational field strength is measured in newtons per kilogram (N/kg), and is numerically equal to the local acceleration due to gravity (m/s^2 and N/kg are dimensionally equivalent units). Combining the definition of gravitational field strength with Newton's law of gravitation (F = GMm/r^2, where M is the mass creating the field) gives g = GM/r^2, showing that gravitational field strength around a spherical mass depends only on the mass creating the field and the distance from its centre, not on the mass of the small test object placed within the field. Because of the inverse-square relationship, gravitational field strength decreases rapidly with increasing distance from the central mass, which is why g is measurably (though only slightly) smaller at high altitude than at sea level, and dramatically smaller far out in space.
key_concepts: g = F/m (N/kg)
g = GM/r^2 (from combining with Newton's law of gravitation)
Numerically equal to local acceleration due to gravity

definitions.definition: The gravitational force acting per unit mass at a point within a gravitational field, calculated as g = F/m, measured in N/kg.

variables.m: mass of the object experiencing the force, kg

formulas.name: Gravitational field strength around a spherical mass

variables.r: distance from the centre of the mass, m

worked_examples.problem: Calculate the gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface, given the Earth's mass is 6.0 x 10^24 kg and its radius is 6.4 x 10^6 m (use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2).
steps: Use g = GM/r^2.
worked_examples.answer: Approximately 9.77 N/kg (close to the standard value of 9.8 N/kg)

practical_applications: Calculating weight at different locations, including other planets and altitudes
Understanding variations in g used in precise geophysical surveys
Space mission planning, accounting for changing gravitational field strength with altitude
common_mistakes: Confusing gravitational field strength, g (N/kg), with the gravitational constant, G (N m^2/kg^2), which are different quantities
Assuming gravitational field strength is exactly the same at every point on or near the Earth's surface
misconceptions: That gravitational field strength depends on the mass of the object experiencing the force — since g = GM/r^2 (derived by combining the definition of g with Newton's law of gravitation), gravitational field strength depends only on the mass creating the field and the distance from it, not on the mass of any test object placed within that field, which is why all objects experience the same g at a given location, regardless of their own mass.
tips: Remember gravitational field strength and acceleration due to gravity are numerically equal and can be used interchangeably (N/kg and m/s^2 are equivalent units in this context).

basic: State the equation for gravitational field strength in terms of force and mass.
intermediate: Calculate the gravitational field strength on the surface of the Moon, given its mass is 7.3 x 10^22 kg and its radius is 1.74 x 10^6 m (use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2).
advanced: Explain why gravitational field strength decreases with increasing altitude above the Earth's surface, referring to the equation g = GM/r^2.

exam_questions: Explain why the gravitational field strength experienced by any object at a given point above the Earth's surface does not depend on the object's own mass.

basic: g = F/m.
advanced: As altitude increases, the distance, r, from the centre of the Earth increases; since g = GM/r^2, and r appears squared in the denominator, increasing r causes g to decrease, following an inverse square relationship (though the effect is small for typical altitudes compared with the Earth's radius).
exam: Combining the definition g = F/m with Newton's law of gravitation, F = GMm/r^2, gives g = (GMm/r^2)/m = GM/r^2 — the object's own mass, m, cancels out of this expression entirely, showing that gravitational field strength at a given point depends only on the mass creating the field, M, and the distance from it, r, not on the mass of any object placed at that point.

summary: Gravitational field strength, g, is the gravitational force per unit mass at a point (g = F/m), measured in N/kg. Combined with Newton's law of gravitation, g = GM/r^2, showing it depends only on the mass creating the field and distance, not on the test object's mass.
revision_notes: g = F/m (N/kg)
g = GM/r^2
Independent of the test object's own mass

subject: Physics
title: Gravitational Potential
description: The gravitational potential energy per unit mass at a point in a gravitational field, always negative and increasing (toward zero) with distance from the source mass.
learning_objectives: Define gravitational potential
State and apply the equation for gravitational potential around a spherical mass
Explain why gravitational potential is defined as negative, with zero at infinity
explanation: Gravitational potential, given the symbol V (or sometimes phi), is defined as the gravitational potential energy per unit mass at a point within a gravitational field, calculated as V = -GM/r, where M is the mass creating the field and r is the distance from its centre. Gravitational potential is always negative (for any finite distance from a mass) and increases toward zero as distance, r, approaches infinity, which is taken as the reference point where gravitational potential is defined to be exactly zero. This negative convention reflects the fact that gravitational force is always attractive: energy must be put in (work done against gravity) to move a mass from close to the source mass out to an infinite distance away, meaning any point closer than infinity has a comparatively 'lower' (more negative) potential energy per unit mass. Gravitational potential is a scalar quantity (unlike gravitational field strength, which is a vector), which can make certain calculations, particularly involving multiple masses, more straightforward, since potentials from different sources simply add algebraically.
key_concepts: V = -GM/r (always negative, zero at infinity)
Scalar quantity (potentials from multiple sources add directly)
Negative sign reflects the attractive nature of gravity

definitions.definition: The gravitational potential energy per unit mass at a point within a gravitational field, calculated as V = -GM/r, with zero defined at infinite distance.

variables.r: distance from the centre of the mass, m

worked_examples.problem: Calculate the gravitational potential at a distance of 4.0 x 10^7 m from the centre of the Earth (mass 6.0 x 10^24 kg), using G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
steps: Use V = -GM/r.

practical_applications: Calculating the energy required for spacecraft to escape a planet's gravitational field
Analysing orbital energy and stability in astrophysics
Calculating gravitational potential energy changes for objects moving significant distances (where the uniform-field approximation, GPE = mgh, is no longer valid)
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in the gravitational potential equation
Confusing gravitational potential (a scalar, J/kg) with gravitational potential energy (a scalar, but in joules, specific to a particular mass, not per unit mass)
misconceptions: That a negative gravitational potential represents some kind of 'negative' or nonsensical physical quantity — the negative sign is simply a consequence of the chosen reference point (zero at infinite distance) combined with gravity always being attractive; a more negative potential simply means a location is 'deeper' within the gravitational field (closer to the source mass) and therefore requires more energy input to escape to infinity from that point.
tips: Remember that gravitational potential always increases (becomes less negative, approaching zero) as distance from the source mass increases, reflecting that less energy is needed to move further away, toward the reference point at infinity.

basic: State the equation for gravitational potential, defining each symbol.
intermediate: Explain why gravitational potential is defined to be zero at an infinite distance from a mass, rather than at some other reference point.
advanced: Calculate the gravitational potential at the surface of the Moon (mass 7.3 x 10^22 kg, radius 1.74 x 10^6 m), using G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.

exam_questions: Explain why gravitational potential is always negative at any finite distance from a mass, using the concept of work done against gravity.

basic: V = -GM/r, where V is gravitational potential in J/kg, G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass creating the field in kg, and r is the distance from its centre in m.
intermediate: Infinite distance is chosen as the reference point because it represents the point at which an object experiences no further gravitational influence from the mass at all, providing a single, unambiguous, and universally consistent reference point for comparing gravitational potential at any finite distance.
exam: Since gravitational force is always attractive, positive work must be done (energy input required) to move a mass away from a source mass, out to an infinite distance, against this attractive pull; since gravitational potential is defined to be exactly zero at infinity, and energy had to be added to reach that point from any closer position, any finite distance must therefore represent a lower (more negative) potential energy state per unit mass than the zero reference point at infinity.

summary: Gravitational potential is the gravitational potential energy per unit mass at a point, V = -GM/r, always negative with zero defined at infinite distance. This reflects the energy needed to move a mass away from an attractive gravitational source to infinity.
revision_notes: V = -GM/r (J/kg)
Always negative; zero at infinity
Scalar quantity; potentials from multiple sources add directly

subject: Physics
title: Gravitational Potential Energy (Radial Field)
description: The gravitational potential energy of a mass within a radial (non-uniform) gravitational field, applicable over large distances such as those involved in orbital and space physics.
learning_objectives: State the equation for gravitational potential energy in a radial field
Explain why this equation differs from the simpler GPE = mgh used in a uniform field
Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a mass at a given distance from a large body
explanation: While the simpler equation GPE = mgh (covered in Work, Energy and Power) works well for everyday heights near the Earth's surface, where the gravitational field can be treated as uniform, it becomes increasingly inaccurate over large distances, such as those involved in satellite orbits or interplanetary travel, where the gravitational field strength itself changes significantly with distance (following an inverse square relationship, as covered in Gravitational Field Strength). For these situations, the more general and accurate equation for gravitational potential energy is GPE = -GMm/r, where M is the mass of the large central body (such as a planet), m is the mass of the smaller object, r is the distance between their centres, and G is the gravitational constant. This equation is directly related to gravitational potential, V = -GM/r, since gravitational potential energy is simply gravitational potential multiplied by the mass of the object placed within the field: GPE = Vm. Like gravitational potential itself, this radial-field GPE is always negative for any finite separation, with zero defined at an infinite distance between the two masses.
key_concepts: GPE = -GMm/r (radial field, valid at any distance)
GPE = Vm (gravitational potential x mass)
Always negative; zero at infinite separation

definitions.definition: The gravitational potential energy of a mass at a distance r from a large central mass M, calculated as GPE = -GMm/r, valid for any distance and always negative, with zero defined at infinite separation.

variables.M: mass of the large central body, kg
variables.m: mass of the smaller object, kg
variables.r: distance between the centres of the two masses, m

worked_examples.problem: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite at a distance of 7.0 x 10^6 m from the centre of the Earth (mass 6.0 x 10^24 kg), using G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
steps: Use GPE = -GMm/r.

practical_applications: Calculating the total energy of satellites and spacecraft in orbit
Determining the energy required for interplanetary missions and gravitational slingshot manoeuvres
Understanding the energy changes involved in a spacecraft escaping a planet's gravitational field entirely
common_mistakes: Applying the simpler GPE = mgh equation over very large distances, where g cannot be treated as constant
Forgetting the negative sign, or incorrectly interpreting what a negative GPE value physically represents
misconceptions: That GPE = mgh and GPE = -GMm/r are simply two unrelated formulas for the same quantity that happen to both exist — GPE = mgh is actually a close approximation of the more general GPE = -GMm/r equation, valid specifically for small height changes near a large body's surface, where g can be treated as approximately constant; the two are connected rather than entirely separate.
tips: Use GPE = mgh only for relatively small height changes near a planet's surface, where g is approximately constant; use GPE = -GMm/r for any situation involving large distances or significant changes in gravitational field strength, such as orbital mechanics.

basic: State the equation for gravitational potential energy in a radial field, defining each symbol.
intermediate: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a 1000 kg spacecraft at a distance of 1.0 x 10^7 m from the centre of the Earth (mass 6.0 x 10^24 kg), using G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
advanced: Explain why the gravitational potential energy of an object increases (becomes less negative) as it moves further from a planet, connecting this to the work done against gravity.

exam_questions: Explain why the equation GPE = mgh is not suitable for calculating the gravitational potential energy change of a satellite moving between two very different orbital altitudes, and state the equation that should be used instead.

basic: GPE = -GMm/r, where GPE is gravitational potential energy in J, G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass of the large central body in kg, m is the mass of the smaller object in kg, and r is the distance between their centres in m.
advanced: As an object moves further from the planet, work must be done against the attractive gravitational force to increase the separation; this work done is transferred to the object's gravitational potential energy, increasing it (making it less negative, moving toward zero as r approaches infinity), consistent with the object needing to gain energy to move to a position of higher (less negative) gravitational potential energy.
exam: GPE = mgh assumes gravitational field strength, g, remains approximately constant over the height change involved, which is a reasonable approximation only for small height changes near a planet's surface; for a satellite moving between very different orbital altitudes, g changes significantly (following an inverse square relationship) over that range, so the more general equation GPE = -GMm/r, which accounts for this changing field strength, must be used instead.

summary: Gravitational potential energy in a radial field is GPE = -GMm/r, valid at any distance from a large mass, unlike the approximate GPE = mgh used for small heights near a surface. It is always negative, with zero defined at infinite separation.
revision_notes: GPE = -GMm/r (radial field, any distance)
GPE = mgh is an approximation, valid only for small height changes near a surface
Always negative; zero at infinite separation

subject: Physics
title: Gravitational Fields
description: The region of space surrounding a mass within which another mass would experience a gravitational force, represented visually using field lines.
learning_objectives: Define a gravitational field
Describe how gravitational field lines represent the direction and strength of a gravitational field
Distinguish a uniform gravitational field from a radial gravitational field
explanation: A gravitational field is the region of space surrounding a mass within which another mass placed at any point would experience a gravitational force of attraction. Gravitational fields are represented visually using gravitational field lines, which show the direction a small test mass would be pulled at any given point (always pointing toward the source mass, since gravity is always attractive), with the spacing of the lines indicating the relative strength of the field — closely spaced lines represent a stronger field, while widely spaced lines represent a weaker field. Around a single, isolated spherical mass (such as a planet), the field lines point radially inward toward the centre of the mass from every direction, becoming more widely spaced (indicating a weakening field) further from the source; this is called a radial field. Very close to the surface of a large body, over a small enough region (such as the surface of the Earth in everyday, small-scale situations), the field lines can be treated as approximately parallel and evenly spaced, an approximation known as a uniform field, which underlies the simpler GPE = mgh and constant g approximations used in introductory mechanics.
key_concepts: Gravitational field: region where a mass experiences gravitational force
Field lines: point toward the source mass, spacing shows relative strength
Radial field (around a point/spherical mass) vs uniform field (small region near a large surface, approximation)

definitions.definition: The region of space surrounding a mass within which another mass would experience a gravitational force.
An approximation of a gravitational field, valid over a small region near a large mass's surface, in which the field lines are treated as parallel and evenly spaced, and g is treated as constant.

worked_examples.problem: Describe the difference in appearance between the gravitational field lines around an isolated planet (viewed from a large distance) and the gravitational field lines just above the Earth's surface, over a small local area (such as a school laboratory).
steps: Around an isolated planet, viewed from a large distance, the field lines point radially inward toward the centre of the planet from every direction, and clearly converge (get closer together) as they approach the centre — a radial field.

Just above the Earth's surface, over a small local area, the curvature of these radial lines is far too gradual to notice, so the field lines appear to be parallel to each other and pointing straight down, evenly spaced — a uniform field approximation.
worked_examples.answer: The full radial field around an isolated planet shows converging field lines pointing toward its centre, while the small-scale view near the Earth's surface approximates this as parallel, evenly-spaced, downward-pointing lines (a uniform field).

practical_applications: Visualising and communicating the strength and direction of gravitational effects in astrophysics and engineering
Justifying the use of the simpler GPE = mgh and constant g approximations for everyday, small-scale physics problems
Comparing gravitational fields around different astronomical bodies
common_mistakes: Assuming the uniform field approximation is valid over very large distances, rather than only very close to a large body's surface
Drawing gravitational field lines pointing away from a mass, rather than toward it (a common error, since some other field types, such as certain electric fields, do point outward)
misconceptions: That the Earth's gravitational field is genuinely uniform, rather than radial — the Earth's true gravitational field is radial (field lines converge toward its centre), and only appears uniform as a very good, useful approximation over the small distances typically involved in everyday, small-scale physics problems near its surface.
tips: Remember gravitational field lines always point toward the source mass (since gravity is only ever attractive), and their spacing (closer = stronger, wider = weaker) shows the relative strength of the field at different points.

basic: State the direction in which gravitational field lines point, relative to the source mass.
intermediate: Explain why gravitational field lines around an isolated planet get closer together nearer to the planet's surface.
advanced: Explain why the uniform field approximation is reasonable for a school laboratory experiment, but would not be reasonable for calculating a satellite's motion at a very high orbital altitude.

exam_questions: Sketch, in words, the gravitational field lines around an isolated spherical planet, and explain what the spacing of these lines represents.

basic: Toward the source mass (inward).
intermediate: Field line spacing represents the relative strength of the gravitational field, with closer spacing indicating a stronger field; since gravitational field strength increases closer to a planet's centre (by g = GM/r^2), the field lines must correspondingly become more closely spaced as they approach the surface.
advanced: Over the small height range involved in a school laboratory (typically a few metres), the change in distance from the Earth's centre is negligibly small compared with the Earth's radius, so g barely changes and can reasonably be treated as constant (a uniform field); at a very high orbital altitude, however, the distance from the Earth's centre may change very significantly relative to the Earth's radius, causing g to vary substantially, so the uniform field approximation would introduce significant errors and the full radial field equations must be used instead.
exam: Gravitational field lines around an isolated spherical planet point radially inward, converging toward the centre of the planet from every direction; the spacing of these lines represents the relative strength of the gravitational field at different points, with more closely spaced lines (found nearer the planet's surface/centre) indicating a stronger gravitational field, and more widely spaced lines (found further away) indicating a weaker field.

summary: A gravitational field is the region around a mass where another mass experiences a gravitational force, represented by field lines pointing toward the source, with spacing indicating relative field strength. A radial field describes the true field around a mass; a uniform field is a useful approximation valid over small regions near a large body's surface.
revision_notes: Field lines point toward the source mass
Closer spacing = stronger field
Radial field (true) vs uniform field (small-region approximation)

subject: Physics
title: Escape Velocity
description: The minimum speed an object must be given to completely escape a body's gravitational field, without any further propulsion.
learning_objectives: Define escape velocity
Derive the equation for escape velocity using conservation of energy
Calculate the escape velocity for a given astronomical body
explanation: Escape velocity is the minimum speed an object must be launched at, from the surface of a planet or other astronomical body, to completely escape that body's gravitational field and never fall back, assuming no further propulsion or energy input after launch, and ignoring air resistance. Escape velocity can be derived using conservation of energy: an object has just enough energy to escape if its initial kinetic energy exactly equals the magnitude of its (negative) gravitational potential energy at the surface, since this allows it to reach an infinite distance (where GPE = 0) with exactly zero kinetic energy remaining. Setting (1/2)mv^2 = GMm/r (the magnitude of GPE at the surface) and solving for v gives the escape velocity equation, v(escape) = root(2GM/r), where M is the mass of the body being escaped and r is the distance from its centre (typically its radius, for launch from the surface). Escape velocity depends only on the mass and radius of the astronomical body, not on the mass of the escaping object, and it is worth noting that 'escape velocity' describes the minimum initial speed needed, not a speed that must be continuously maintained.
key_concepts: Minimum speed to escape a gravitational field entirely (no further propulsion)
Derived from conservation of energy: KE = |GPE| at the surface
v(escape) = root(2GM/r); independent of the escaping object's own mass

definitions.definition: The minimum speed an object must be given to completely escape a body's gravitational field, without further propulsion, calculated as v(escape) = root(2GM/r).

variables.M: mass of the body being escaped, kg
variables.r: distance from the centre of the body (often its radius), m

worked_examples.problem: Derive the escape velocity equation, v(escape) = root(2GM/r), starting from conservation of energy.
steps: At the minimum escape condition, the object's initial kinetic energy exactly equals the magnitude of its gravitational potential energy at the surface: (1/2)mv^2 = GMm/r.
Cancel the mass, m, from both sides: (1/2)v^2 = GM/r.
Multiply both sides by 2: v^2 = 2GM/r.
Take the square root of both sides: v = root(2GM/r).
worked_examples.answer: v(escape) = root(2GM/r), and since m cancels, this is independent of the escaping object's own mass.

worked_examples.problem: Calculate the escape velocity from the Earth's surface, given the Earth's mass is 6.0 x 10^24 kg and radius 6.4 x 10^6 m (use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2).
steps: Use v(escape) = root(2GM/r).

practical_applications: Calculating the launch speed required for spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit entirely, such as for interplanetary missions
Explaining why some planets and moons cannot retain certain gases in their atmosphere (if average molecular speeds approach the escape velocity)
Understanding the physics of black holes, where escape velocity would need to exceed the speed of light
common_mistakes: Assuming escape velocity must be continuously maintained throughout the entire journey away from a planet, rather than being the minimum required initial launch speed
Forgetting to include the factor of 2 in the escape velocity equation (a very common error, confusing it with the orbital speed equation)
misconceptions: That reaching escape velocity means an object is 'immune' to further gravitational influence — an object launched at exactly escape velocity is still slowed down by gravity throughout its entire journey away from the planet, but has just enough initial kinetic energy that its speed only reaches exactly zero as it approaches an infinite distance, meaning it will never fall back, without needing any further propulsion after launch.
tips: Remember the escape velocity derivation relies on the object's kinetic energy exactly matching the magnitude of its (negative) gravitational potential energy, so that its total energy (KE + GPE) is exactly zero — the minimum total energy needed to reach an infinite distance.

basic: State the equation for escape velocity, defining each symbol.
intermediate: Calculate the escape velocity from the Moon's surface, given its mass is 7.3 x 10^22 kg and radius 1.74 x 10^6 m (use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2).
advanced: Explain why escape velocity does not depend on the direction in which an object is launched (ignoring air resistance and the shape of the astronomical body).

exam_questions: Explain, using the principle of conservation of energy, why an object launched at exactly the escape velocity from a planet's surface will just barely reach an infinite distance with zero remaining kinetic energy.

basic: v(escape) = root(2GM/r), where v(escape) is escape velocity in m/s, G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass of the body being escaped in kg, and r is the distance from its centre in m.
advanced: Escape velocity is derived purely from energy considerations (total energy exactly equal to zero) and the object's distance from the centre of the astronomical body, neither of which inherently depends on the direction of launch; in practice, however, launching in certain directions (such as with the rotation of the planet) can provide a useful additional boost to the object's actual speed relative to space, even though the underlying escape velocity value itself, based purely on distance from the centre, does not change with direction.
exam: By conservation of energy, an object's total energy (kinetic + gravitational potential) remains constant as it moves away from the planet, assuming no other forces do work on it; if launched with kinetic energy exactly equal in magnitude to its initial (negative) gravitational potential energy, its total energy is exactly zero, and since gravitational potential energy approaches zero as distance approaches infinity, conservation of energy requires that its kinetic energy must also approach zero at that same infinite distance, meaning the object's speed decreases continuously but never quite reaches zero before infinity, and never falls back.

summary: Escape velocity is the minimum initial speed needed to completely escape a body's gravitational field, calculated as v(escape) = root(2GM/r) using conservation of energy. It depends only on the mass and radius of the body being escaped, not on the escaping object's own mass.
revision_notes: v(escape) = root(2GM/r)
Derived from KE = |GPE| at the surface (total energy = 0)
Independent of the escaping object's own mass
